# Meeting notes {.unnumbered}

This page is the group's shared record of what was actually said. It is public, so keep unpublished results, confidential data, and anything a collaborator has not agreed to share in the private group notes instead.

Add an entry under the meeting you attended. Sign and date it. Do not edit anyone else's entry; disagree by adding your own underneath. The fastest route is the "Edit this page" link in the right-hand margin, which opens this file on GitHub and turns your change into a pull request.

Each session page ends with the same four prompts, and they are the ones worth answering here: the evidence for your main claim, what changed your mind, what remains unresolved, and one change to the agent or its evaluation. A note that records a disagreement is more useful later than one that records a consensus.

## Meeting 1: Is there a scientific method?

*Held: September 15, 2026. Reading: [session page](sessions/01-scientific-method.qmd), with @fortunato2018 and @simon1973 brought into the discussion.*

Transcribed from the group's shared notes, September 23, 2026. The session page gives the full account and the readings checked against the notes.

- Evidence for the main claim: the method as the room stated it is Cleland's schema, H with conditions $C$ implying E; conditions are never fully represented, so falsification in nature is rarely as clean as Platt and Chamberlin describe.
- What changed: the smoking gun was read as both discriminating and biasing toward confirmation; Simon's argument that generating hypotheses is a search, better or worse done, gave the group a way to treat discovery as having a logic.
- Unresolved: whether experimental and historical science differ in kind or in degree; the source and strength of the small-stable-core finding.
- One change to the agent: log how each rival at H was generated, so that search strategies can be compared.
- Follow-up, September 23: the discussion of prior knowledge traced to @klahr1999, read in full. It gives the unit graph its surprise edge and a sixth entry state (graph v0.3).

## Meeting 10: Scientific novelty: new to whom, compared with what?

*Held: September 22, 2026. Reading: [session page](sessions/10-novelty.qmd), with @hofstra2020, @machado2026, and @si2025 presented alongside the anchor.*

Transcribed from the group's shared notes and slides, September 23, 2026. The session page gives the full account and the readings checked against the notes.

- Evidence for the main claim: Uzzi's high-impact pattern is a conventional base with an atypical tail; Hofstra separates novelty from uptake and finds them pulling in opposite directions, with uptake falling as link distance grows.
- What changed: "novelty" was used for at least four constructs (journal-pair atypicality, new concept links, embedding distance, expert rating against anchors). The group asked for a subjective and an objective rubric, kept side by side.
- Position taken: human–AI teams raise novelty and breadth; agents raise uptake and impact, taking up new links without waiting for a local human audience.
- Unresolved: whether an agent audience takes up distal links or reproduces the discount on them (Machado); whether distal novelty is taken up less in the earth sciences; whether novelty drives impact once a long citation window is used.
- One change to the agent: record novelty and expected uptake as separate fields, and the distance of any link generated at H.
